scenes.title: Why Airplane Food Tastes Worse
scenes.subtitle: Explained in 90 seconds
scenes.narration: You've probably noticed this. The same meal, in the air, just doesn't taste right. Here's why.

scenes.subtitle: At cruising altitude, your body is in a **pressurized cabin** at 8,000 feet.
scenes.narration: At cruising altitude, your body is sitting in a pressurized cabin equivalent to about eight thousand feet of elevation.

scenes.subtitle: The dry air dehydrates your **nose and tongue**.
scenes.narration: The air inside the cabin is drier than the Sahara Desert, which dries out your nose and tongue almost the moment you board.

scenes.fact: Your sense of taste for sweet and salty drops by up to 30% in flight.
scenes.narration: Studies commissioned by Lufthansa found your ability to taste sweet and salty drops by as much as thirty percent at altitude.

scenes.subtitle: Cabin noise also dulls **sweetness** and boosts **umami**.
scenes.narration: And there's another twist. The constant low rumble of the engines suppresses your perception of sweetness while actually amplifying umami flavors.

scenes.subtitle: That's why airlines load their food with **salt, spice, and tomato**.
scenes.narration: That's why airlines pack their meals with extra salt, extra spice, and a surprising amount of tomato juice — they're compensating for taste buds that simply aren't working right.
